newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan firms anxious but not reviewing Peru plans.
newsitem.headline: Japan firms anxious but not reviewing Peru plans.

text.p: Japanese firms caught up in the hostage crisis in Peru awaited for word on captive workers on Thursday but said it was too early to review business plans in the country.
The Japanese Chamber of Commerce and Industry denied media reports it had cancelled plans to send a large mission to Peru and neighbouring Latin American nations in September 1997.
"We are collecting information and have made no decision yet," a spokesman said.

Japanese firms with staff held hostage by leftist rebels since Tuesday night at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima included Toyota Motor Corp, Matsushita Electric Industrial Co Ltd, Mitsui Mining and Smelting Co Ltd, Nissho Iwai Corp, Mitsui & Co Ltd, Marubeni Corp, Mitsubishi Corp and NEC Corp.

Mostly Peru branch directors, the Japanese executives were among 484 diplomats and Peruvian government officials held captive by guerrillas from the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), which has said it will kill them if Peru fails to free 400 to 500 of its jailed comrades.

The firms were part of Japan's substantial business presence in mineral-rich Peru, where Japanese industry -- mostly mining concerns -- had invested a cumulative $764 million as of 1995, according to Japanese government figures.
Mitsui Mining and Smelting Co said it had no immediate plan to review its mining business in Peru.
"Six of our employees are still held as hostages. But at this stage we have no immediate plan to review or withdraw from mining business in Peru," a Mitsui Mining spokesman told Reuters.
Since 1964, Mitsui Mining and Mitsui & Co Ltd have jointly run Huanzala mine in Peru, which produces 75,000 tonnes of zinc ore and 25,000 tonnes of lead ore per year.
"One of our employees successfully called us to say they're fine," the Mitsui Mining spokesman said.
Japan's Foreign Ministry on Thursday briefed local companies on the hostage crisis in Lima and promised to keep the firms fully informed about new developments.
In 1995, Peru's exports to Japan -- mostly minerals -- were worth $541 million, while Lima imported some $300 million worth of cars, electronics and machinery from Japan.

Peru was the leading recipient of Japanese development loans to Latin America, receiving 31.8 billion yen ($281 million) in 1995, the latest year for which complete figures were available. Japan's grant aid to Peru was 3.64 billion yen in 1995.
